title-group.article-title: Prognostic impact of frailty based on a comprehensive frailty assessment in patients with heart failure

sec.title: Aims
sec.p: This study aimed to evaluate the impact of frailty and living function domains based on the Kihon Checklist (KCL), a questionnaire for a comprehensive frailty assessment, on prognosis in patients with acute heart failure (AHF).

sec.title: Methods and results
sec.p: The Kochi Registry of Subjects with Acute Decompensated Heart Failure (Kochi YOSACOI) study was a prospective multicentre cohort study enrolling 1061 patients hospitalized for AHF from May 2017 to December 2019 in Japan. We divided patients into three groups according to the severity of frailty using the KCL and compared clinical outcomes after discharge. The primary endpoint was all‐cause death, and the secondary outcomes were cardiovascular death, heart failure (HF) rehospitalization, and the composite event of cardiovascular death and HF rehospitalization. Of 936 patients (median age, 81 years; 48.9% women) who could be assessed for frailty, we identified frailty in 501 patients (53.5%), prefrailty in 290 patients (31.0%), and non‐frailty in 145 patients (15.5%). Compared with prefrail and non‐frail patients, frail patients were older (83 vs. 79 and 72 years, P < 0.001), were more likely to be women (53.9% vs. 43.1% and 43.4%, P = 0.005), and were more likely to have a history of previous HF hospitalization (35.4% vs. 25.3% and 19.6%, P < 0.001) and multimorbidity (90.8% vs. 81.0% and 73.8%, P < 0.001). Frail patients had a lower rate of discharge to home (79.7% vs. 94.8% and 96.5%, P < 0.001). During the 2 year follow‐up period, frail patients had a higher incidence rate of all‐cause death, cardiovascular death, and HF rehospitalization (log‐rank P < 0.001, P < 0.001, and P = 0.003, respectively). After adjusting for other prognostic factors, multivariate analysis showed that frailty was associated with all‐cause death [adjusted hazard ratio (HR): 2.917, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.326–6.417, P = 0.008] and cardiovascular death (adjusted HR: 7.026, 95% CI: 1.700–29.030, P = 0.007). Among all domains of the KCL, the cognitive function domain was associated with a higher risk of all‐cause death (P = 0.004) and cardiovascular death (P < 0.001). The depression domain remained associated with a higher risk of HF rehospitalization (P = 0.045). The risk for all‐cause death increased with an increase in total KCL score (adjusted HR: 1.819, 95% CI: 1.300–2.547, P < 0.001).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The KCL is a useful tool for risk stratification of adverse outcomes in patients with AHF. Functional declines in psycho‐emotional domains including cognitive function and depressed mood contribute to adverse outcomes.
Keywords: Frailty, Acute heart failure, Older adults, Comprehensive geriatric assessment, Prognosis, Functional ability

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The number of patients with heart failure (HF) continues to increase worldwide, and HF is one of the leading causes of death and hospitalization in developed countries. The prevalence of HF increases with aging, and 6–10% of people older than 65 years of age have the disorder. 1 , 2 The population of Japan is among the most aged in the world, with an aging rate of 29% in 2021. 3 Therefore, along with the increase in the number of patients with HF, the aging of patients with HF is also increasing. Frailty is characterized by vulnerability, in which the physiological reserve against external stress is reduced. 4 The prevalence of frailty increases with age, and its prognosis is adversely affected by cardiovascular diseases. 5 Frailty is one of the most important health problems in the elderly as it is associated with poor outcomes such as necessity for long‐term care, hospitalization, institutionalization, and death. 6 Frail patients have vulnerabilities in various domains, including physical, cognitive, mental, and social domains, which can be barriers to disease management in HF. Therefore, we need to comprehensively assess frailty in HF patients and provide appropriate interventions in declining functional domains. The Kihon Checklist (KCL) has been validated as a comprehensive frailty assessment and is widely used in Japan as a comprehensive geriatric assessment. 7 , 8 The purpose of the present study was to investigate the impact of frailty status and daily functional domains based on the KCL on prognosis in patients with acute heart failure (AHF).

sec.title: Study design and patient population
sec.p: This study was a prospective multicentre observational cohort study in the Kochi Registry of Subjects with Acute Decompensated Heart Failure (Kochi YOSACOI) study. We used data for 1061 patients with AHF who were enrolled between May 2017 and December 2019. Details of the Kochi YOSACOI study have been previously described. 9 Briefly, the Kochi YOSACOI study consists of six hospitals providing acute care for cardiovascular diseases in Kochi Prefecture. In this region, 36% of the population is 65 years of age or older, making it the most aged region in Japan. We enrolled patients aged 20 years or older who were hospitalized for AHF at six participating hospitals. The diagnosis of AHF was based on the presence of at least two major criteria or one major criterion in conjunction with two minor criteria in the Framingham criteria. Patients under 20 years of age and those who did not consent to registry enrolment were excluded. Patients who were not assessed by the KCL during hospitalization and patients without prognostic information during follow‐up were excluded. Clinical information on all patients was collected by investigators at each participating hospital at the time of enrolment in the registry.

The Kochi YOSACOI study was conducted in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare's Ethnical Guidelines for Medical and Health Research Involving Human Subjects. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee on Medical Research of Kochi Medical School (Approval Number 28‐68) and the ethics committees of all participating hospitals. Informed consent was obtained from all patients or their proxies according to the guidelines of the Ethics Committee on Medical Research of Kochi Medical School.

sec.title: Data collection and definitions
sec.p:
Clinical information on all patients was collected by investigators at each participating hospital at the time of enrolment in the registry. We obtained information on baseline characteristics, underlying diseases, comorbidities, results of laboratory examinations, results of echocardiographic examinations, nutritional status, physical frailty status, cognitive impairment, the KCL, and medication at discharge. 9 In Japan, the KCL is widely used by local governments to assess older adults' health status and life functions. The information obtained is used for the prevention of long‐term care for older adults. The KCL questionnaire consists of 25 simple questions reflecting seven functional domains: instrumental activities of daily living (IADL), physical function, nutritional status, oral function, socialization, cognitive function, and depressive mood (Supporting Information, Table
S1 ). The KCL is a validated measure for frail assessment methods. 7 In the present study, we defined total KCL scores of ≥8 points as frailty, 4–7 points as prefrailty, and 0–3 points as non‐frailty, according to a previous study. 7 Each of the seven living functional domains of the KCL also has cut‐off points for assessing functional decline that were defined in a previous report. 8 We defined the cut‐off points for each of the seven living functional domains of the KCL to functional decline as follows: IADL domain ≥ 3 points, physical function domain ≥ 3 points, malnutrition domain = 2 points, oral function domain ≥ 2 points, socialization domain ≥ 1 point, cognitive function domain ≥ 1 point, and depression domain ≥ 2 points.

sec.title: Clinical outcomes
sec.p: Data for the prognosis of patients within 2 years of discharge were obtained prospectively. The primary endpoint of this study was defined as all‐cause death. We assessed cardiovascular death, rehospitalization due to worsening HF, and the composite event of cardiovascular death and rehospitalization due to worsening HF within 2 years of discharge as secondary endpoints. Cardiovascular death was defined as sudden cardiac death in patients with a relatively stable condition in whom unexpected sudden collapse occurred, death from worsening HF, death from acute myocardial infarction, and death from vascular disease and stroke. HF rehospitalization was defined as the first hospitalization after discharge due to worsening HF that was judged to require hospitalization by the cardiologist at the participating hospital.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Continuous variables are expressed as means ± standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs) and were compared by using a one‐way analysis of variance when normally distributed or by using the Kruskal–Wallis test when not normally distributed. Categorical variables are expressed as numbers with percentages and were compared using Pearson's χ 2 test. Fisher's exact test was used when the expected frequency was lower than 5. Kaplan–Meier analyses were used to estimate the incidence of clinical events after discharge, and differences in the event incidences in patients with frailty, prefrailty, and non‐frailty were estimated by the log‐rank test. Univariable and multivariable analyses using a Cox proportional hazard regression model were conducted to estimate the association of frailty status with clinical events. We adjusted the models for age, gender, systolic blood pressure at discharge, prior HF rehospitalization, serum brain natriuretic peptide level at discharge, estimated glomerular filtration rate < 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, sodium, haemoglobin level, use of renin‐angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors and beta‐blockers, New York Heart Association class III/IV at discharge, diabetes mellitus, and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), which were identified in previous studies as potential risk factors of all‐cause death and rehospitalization due to worsening HF. 10 , 11 , 12 Moreover, a multivariate logistic regression analysis was conducted to estimate the associations of the seven domains in the KCL with the incidence of clinical events. Patients with missing data were excluded from these analyses. Sensitivity analysis was performed for assessment of the association between the total KCL score and all‐cause death using the Cox proportional hazard model and a cubic spline curve in which the total KCL score was treated as a continuous variable. Statistical significance was defined by two‐sided P ≤ 0.05. All statistical analyses were performed using EZR (Saitama Medical Center, Jichi Medical University, Saitama, Japan) on R Commander Version 2.7‐1 13 and RStudio Version 2022.12.0+353 (RStudio PBC, Boston, MA, USA).

sec.title: Clinical characteristics
sec.p:
Among 1061 patients enrolled in the Kochi YOSACOI study, 936 patients (88.2%) were evaluated by the KCL and had follow‐up data available. In the 936 patients, we identified frailty in 501 patients (53.5%), prefrailty in 290 patients (31.0%), and non‐frailty in 145 patients (15.5%) (Figure 1 ). The demographic and clinical characteristics of the patients according to their frailty status are shown in Table
1 . Overall, the median age of the patients at registration was 81 years (IQR, 72–87 years), and 458 patients (48.9%) were women. The proportion of patients aged 80 years or older was 55%. Patients with frailty were older, more likely to be women, had a lower body mass index at discharge, and were more likely to have severe HF symptoms at discharge, a longer length of hospital stay, and a lower rate of discharge to home. Patients with frailty were more likely to have multimorbidity and a history of previous hospitalizations for HF. Comorbidities such as atrial fibrillation or flutter, cerebral vascular accidents, and chronic kidney disease were more common in patients with frailty. Patients with frailty had lower serum albumin, lower haemoglobin, lower estimated glomerular filtration rate, and higher blood urea nitrogen. Regarding medications at discharge, patients with frailty had lower prescription rates of RAS inhibitors and beta‐blockers and higher prescription rates of loop diuretics and tolvaptan.

sec.title: Impact of frailty on clinical outcomes
sec.p:
Among the patients with frailty, those with prefrailty, and those with non‐frailty, the incidence rates of all‐cause death (28.9%, 15.5%, and 6.2%, respectively, P < 0.001), cardiovascular death (14.8%, 7.9%, and 1.4%, respectively, P < 0.001), HF rehospitalization (36.5%, 33.8%, and 23.4%, respectively, P = 0.013), and combined events of cardiovascular death and HF rehospitalization (40.9%, 35.9%, and 24.1%, respectively, P = 0.001) during a 2 year period after discharge were higher in patients with frailty. Kaplan–Meier analysis showed that patients with frailty and those with prefrailty had higher risks of all‐cause death and cardiovascular death than the risks for patients with non‐frailty (Figure 2 ). Regarding HF rehospitalization and the composite of cardiovascular death and HF rehospitalization, patients with frailty had a higher risk than those with non‐frailty. The results of univariate and multivariate analyses using Cox proportional hazard models for adverse outcomes stratified by frailty status are shown in Table
2 . The univariate analysis showed that frailty and prefrailty were significantly associated with all‐cause death, cardiovascular death, HF rehospitalization, and the composite event of cardiovascular death and HF rehospitalization. The multivariate analysis showed that frailty was significantly associated with all‐cause death, cardiovascular death, and the composite event of cardiovascular death and HF rehospitalization.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This is the first study in which the association between a comprehensive frailty assessment using the KCL and prognosis in HF patients was investigated. The results showed that frail patients with HF were at greater risk for all‐cause death, cardiovascular death, HF rehospitalization, and the composite endpoint of cardiovascular death and HF rehospitalization. Among the seven domains of the KCL, the cognitive function domain was associated with all‐cause death and cardiovascular death, and the depression domain was associated with HF rehospitalization. The risk of all‐cause death increased with an increase in the total KCL score.

Several studies have shown that frailty is associated with worse clinical outcomes and functional impairment in the HF population. 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 However, many different methods were used for evaluating frailty status, including methods that evaluate only a physical phenotype and methods that evaluate multiple domains from multidimensional aspects. There are still no internationally established assessment tools and diagnostic criteria for frailty. Frailty evaluated by different methods, however, has been shown to have a negative impact on the prognosis of patients with HF. Multidimensional assessment of frailty would enable identification of individual domains of functional domains and progressive factors for frailty, which may lead to improvement in the quality of life and prognosis through intervention. 18 , 19 In Japan, the KCL was developed to screen community‐dwelling elderly persons aged 65 years or over for daily living functions and to provide intervention in each domain of functional decline. The KCL was also proven to be a useful tool for assessing frailty in the elderly. 7 In our study, when patients hospitalized for AHF were assessed for frailty using the KCL, 54% were frail, 31% were prefrail, and only 15% were non‐frail. 9 Approximately 40–50% of the HF patients had functional declines in the domains of physical function, cognitive function, and depression. Therefore, assessments of not only physical function but also cognitive function and mental status should be performed for HF patients, most of whom are primarily elderly. Several clinical guidelines recommend that assessment and intervention are necessary not only in medical aspects but also in psychological and social aspects for managing HF. 20 , 21 , 22 The JCARE‐CARD study showed that daily management and self‐management accounted for half of the factors associated with rehospitalization due to worsening HF. 23 The KCL may be useful for identifying patients at high risk for poor disease management because various domains of daily living functions can be easily assessed through a simple questionnaire. In this study, patients with frailty had higher incidences of all‐cause death, cardiovascular death, and HF rehospitalization than did patients with non‐frailty. While possible reasons may be that patients with frailty are older, have more comorbidities, are more severely ill, and have poorer nutritional status, it is thought that declines in multiple domains of daily living functions lead to inadequate disease management and a worse prognosis. In patients with HF, a comprehensive assessment of daily living functions using the KCL and appropriate interventions based on the assessment may contribute to improvement of disease management and the reduction of adverse events. The FRAGILE‐HF study showed that the accumulation of multiple domains of frailty, such as physical, cognitive, and social aspects, was associated with a poor prognosis. Although the method of assessing frailty used in the study differs from ours, the findings that the accumulation of declined domains was associated with poor outcomes are consistent with those of our study. 24 In this study, we showed that functional declines, particularly in the mental and cognitive function domains, were associated with poor outcomes. In previous studies, the prevalence of cognitive impairment in the HF cohort was approximately 40%, and the prevalence of depression was approximately 20–30%. 25 , 26 Those studies showed that cognitive impairment and depression were associated with adverse outcomes in patients with HF. 25 , 26 Cognitive impairment and depression can have a negative impact on the self‐care abilities of patients with HF and ultimately lead to poor outcomes. 27 In this study, declines in the cognitive function and depression domains were most associated with poor outcomes among all domains of living function. The cognitive impairment and depressive mood assessed by the KCL have not been adequately validated. However, based on these findings, we believe that the KCL is a useful screening tool for managing patients with HF.

The questions in the KCL questionnaire are designed to reflect the daily living conditions of older people, and interventions and support are needed in the domains in which functional decline has been determined. In addition, in community‐dwelling older people, assessment using the KCL has been reported to be useful for predicting care and support needs and functional disability in the future. 28 , 29 , 30 Impaired daily living function leads to poor medication adherence at home and poor disease management in HF. Appropriate intervention in the domains of impaired daily function assessed by the KCL may improve the quality of disease management. The KCL is a simple and useful tool for stratifying the risk of adverse outcomes in individual patients and identifying domains of daily living function that should be targeted for intervention.

sec.title: Study limitations
sec.p: There are several limitations to be acknowledged. First, the patient population is not large for a cohort study of HF patients. However, patients with HF were enrolled in our registry at major facilities in Kochi Prefecture. Therefore, the findings of this study may approximately reflect the status of patients with HF in our aging region. The relationships between frailty status and adverse events in patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction, HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction, and HF with preserved ejection fraction, respectively, could not be analysed due to an insufficient patient population. However, multivariate analysis using LVEF as a covariate showed that frailty was associated with poorer outcomes compared with non‐frailty. We had collected information on valvular disease as a major cause of AHF but not detailed information on valvular disease. We also did not have data on right ventricular function. Therefore, it is not possible to examine whether they affected the relationship between frailty and prognosis. Second, the KCL questionnaire is a self‐administered questionnaire, and the KCL scores may not be accurate in patients with severe HF or cognitive impairment. Also, patients with advanced dementia and patients who were unable to respond to the questions were excluded from this study. The assessment based on the KCL in the present study reflected living functional status before hospitalization and may not reflect changes during hospitalization and after discharge. The KCL questionnaire is a simple questionnaire that can be repeated, and it is necessary to re‐evaluate the KCL after discharge and reflect it in the intervention in clinical practice. Third, the current clinical guideline recommends the use of angiotensin receptor‐neprilysin inhibitors and sodium‐glucose transporter 2 inhibitors for patients with HF. Patients were enrolled in our registry at a time when these drugs were not available in Japan. Finally, assessment of each domain of living functions based on the KCL has not been adequately validated in patients with HF. In this study, functional decline in cognitive function and depression domains was associated with adverse outcomes. However, assessment by the KCL alone may not be sufficient for diagnosing cognitive impairment and depression. The KCL is used by a department of health and welfare of a local government in Japan to identify elderly people at high risk for the requirement of long‐term care. The cognitive function domain of the KCL was associated with the incidence of dementia. 19 The questions in the questionnaire for the depression domain reflect a depressive mood and may be useful for identifying older adults at high risk for a depressed mood. Therefore, these assessments may be useful for identifying patients at risk for cognitive impairment and depression.

sec.title: Future research
sec.p: This study showed that frailty, diagnosed on the basis of an assessment of daily living function, was associated with poor outcomes in patients with HF. In patients with frailty or prefrailty, it is necessary to examine whether interventions for individual domains of impaired living function can improve impaired living function and frailty status. In addition, it is necessary to consider whether that improvement will reduce the need for support and care, institutionalization, mortality, and HF rehospitalization.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The KCL is a useful tool for risk stratification of adverse outcomes after discharge and for frailty assessment based on the assessment of daily living functions in patients with AHF. Considering that functional declines in the psycho‐emotional domains, including cognitive function and depressive mood, were shown to contribute to adverse outcomes in elderly patients with HF, appropriate interventions for these domains should be attempted to improve the prognosis.
